Mr. Speaker, in speaking on this matter I am going to try to represent the opinions of my own section of the country and at the same time be true to the oath of office which I took before occupying my seat in this house.
There is no doubt that when the article in question appeared in Maclean's magazine last September, the article with which the whole country is now familiar, the minds of the Canadian people were troubled. A good many of them did not see that article when it was first published, but I believe later on the publishers of Maclean's magazine found it possible to spread the article into every section of the country. To anyone who took the trouble to read it, however, it was plain that it contained no concise accusations but only insinuations against people in the public life of this country, more particularly in regard to the
'Mr. Mackenzie King.]
Department of National Defence. Something had to be done; the newspapers were asking for action on the part of the government. Then, a very few days following the publication of the article, the newspapers of Canada were unanimous in praising the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for appointing a royal commission. That step was taken at once, and by that action the Prime Minister and the government showed themselves ready and willing to get to the bottom of all these insinuations or so-called accusations.
On Friday of last week the Prime Minister again showed his honesty and sincerity of purpose in connection with all matters having to do with the administration of this country and the government departments when he stated in the house that he did not wish in any way to curtail discussion on any important problem. He also made it clear, however, that the best body to deal impartially with a question such as this was a committee appointed by the House of Commons, which naturally would be the public accounts committee. No one could take objection to or umbrage at such a statement or the taking of such action. Public opinion as expressed by the press of the country was unanimous in commending the action of the Prime Minister on this occasion.
But it is easy to build up partisan capital. The Prime Minister last fall in appointing a royal commissioner was careful to select a man who-not mentioning his political affiliations-was highly respected in his own profession and had made a name for himself as a lawyer in Canada. However, I was dumbfounded when from every section of the opposition I heard the action of the Prime Minister challenged, and heard the references that were made to his statement not that the commissioner was the supporter of any particular party but simply that he had been appointed by the late administration. I could easily visualize what bitter criticism there would have been had a man been selected who before his appointment had had Liberal inclinations. I repeat that the people have been absolutely satisfied, in their own minds, that the Prime Minister of Canada and the government as a whole wanted to have justice meted out, and to go thoroughly into the accusations that were made.
Frankly in a discussion of this kind I do not like the atmosphere of the House of Commons. Allegations of scandal have been made in a good many instances. I do not believe the country wants to hear discussions of that nature carried on by the opposition for days and weeks.

The leader of the opposition gave us his opinion as to the best speech delivered in the present session on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. To some extent I have no quarrel with him. He said that in his opinion the best speech had been delivered by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil). I cannot agree with him on that score. In my opinion the best speech

from the opposition side was that delivered by the hon. member for Yukon (Mrs. Black). She did not attempt to raise the dust of scandal; she did not try to embarrass the government in its efforts to solve the problems that are facing the country at the present time, although she criticized some of the government's actions. She spoke as a true representative in this parliament of her constituents and the people of Canada. She told the house that some responsibility rested upon the government. That is quite true, but it rests also on all individual members. She also told us she felt that in some instances it was our responsibility that young people of Canada should be told that they had a duty toward themselves as well as toward our institutions as we know them.
The leader of the opposition gave us a sort of lecture which was made up of nothing but insinuations. He made no direct accusation. He made it plain that he was absolutely certain that there was no corruption as far as the Bren gun contract was concerned. I ask and the people, of northern Ontario ask why the time of the house is taken up in this way when we should be trying to solve the problem of unemployment, the problem of agriculture, and the other problems that face this dominion. This action is being taken simply as political strategy on the part of the opposition. I make this declaration and accusation deliberately. The leader of the opposition spoke his mind very openly. He said, speaking of the commissioner, that Davis "did it in a sort of subtle manner." That is a fine phrase to come from the mouth of the leader of the opposition in connection with a matter of this kind. That is a fine thing to say about a man who is recognized as having given his best for successive weeks, and as being absolutely fair to everyone concerned. The present leader of the Conservative party, a party which once was great, has this to say about Mr. Justice Davis. Later on he called this a game. Certainly, it is a game which he has been playing since last Monday. It is a game of political strategy. He said he wanted to go ahead with his story. It was a biased story he told, but not a wonderful story for the people of Canada to read and agree with. If it were possible for all the citizens of Canada to be here during this debate, I am sure they would realize that we are not fulfilling our duties as we should, and that this discussion is absolutely futile.

Let me say a word about the conscription of industry. It is interesting to see the most reactionary party hand in hand with the radical party in this house urging the nationalization of industry. I am quite open-minded on the question of nationalization of war industries. But in Canada we are in the happy position that as far as socialism, communism, fascism and nazism are concerned, we can let other countries experiment with them. As regards munition manufacture we have the experience of France, that great ally of Great Britain. They have their popular front, a radical and labour government; they nationalized their aviation industry, and I refer to a report that was given dealing briefly with that matter.
One of the legacies of the popular front, state manufacture of armaments, has been held responsible for France's weakness in aircraft. This in turn was a compelling factor in the acceptance of the Munich agreement.

This matter that we are debating [DOT]calls for some heart-searching. It behooves every hon. member, whether in the government or the opposition, to do that heart-searching. I will speak on the principle of this question rather than the details and the evidence; the latter has been amply covered by hon. members.
I am mindful of the fact that some twenty years ago almost half a million young men, the flower of Canada's manhood, left these shores to fight for Canada and the empire. They wore army boots on which exorbitant profits had been made, and they ate bully

beef, some of which was not fit to eat, but on the profits of which men at home had waxed sleek and fat. I believe it is the mind and will of every hon. member of this house and every man in a position of leadership in this country and every last man, woman and child in Canada that this shall not be repeated in the year of our Lord 1939. I am equally sure that the brave soldier sitting on the government benches as Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) will do everything humanly possible to see that it does not happen again; for I believe he has qualities of mind and heart that will enable him to do a good job.

I have already told you. If the hon. gentleman would like me to enumerate some of the plants I should be glad to do so. This business was handed for negotiation to a man who had had no experience in the making of munitions of war. It was given to a company which was not equipped to turn out a product of this sort, a firm of very doubtful financial responsibility. I suggest that this is not a very auspicious start in the spending of $63,000,000.
I said that I would not go into the evidence, but inasmuch as some exception has been taken to what I have said I think I ought to refer to one part of Mr. Justice Davis's findings:
Notwithstanding that the contract involves the expenditure of several millions of dollars by the Canadian government, no industrial producer (other than Major Hahn) was confMr. Marsh.]
suited by the Department of National Defence as to the proposed manufacture of Bren guns for the Canadian government or invited to give competitive bids for terms of manufacture. Nor did anyone, so far as the evidence shows, ever visit any industrial plant (except Inglis) to consider the possibility of production of Bren guns in Canada. Mr. Hellmuth put certain questions to the minister in this connection to which, with the answers, I now refer: -
Q. You did not give anybody else a chance?
A. Nobody asked for it.
I will not give what follows; it is simply an elaboration of what I have read. Sir, I would not buy a pair of boots in that way with my own money; how much less should the department use the taxpayers' money to buy instruments of war? I submit that the stewardship of money is not a virtue in the department. If it is they have not shown it in this contract. The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) wrote to the Prime Minister a letter a part of which I will read:
A group of friends of mine in Toronto are equipped fully to manufacture munitions. Their plant is located in my constituency. They have asked me to ascertain whether or not the government's policy permits of the obtaining of orders from the British government. I shall appreciate greatly receiving your advice in this regard.
That is the evidence of the hon. member for Trinity: "We have a plant, we are equipped." Well, now, the resident inspector in Ottawa, appointed as inspector for the department of ordnance, made an honest report with reference to this same plant. Here is the report:
This plant is primarily equipped for the manufacture of boilers, turbines and the working of heavy plate generally. All equipment is in reasonably good condition, considering the length of time it has been in use.
The machinery at present in this factory with few exceptions is unsuited for the manufacture of aircraft, but it might be used for the' manufacture of tanks or shells. . . .
I interject: how much less capable of being used for precision machinery like the Bren gun.
This factory is at present inoperative and has not been in operation since April, 1936. There is no design staff at present employed and the total number of workmen now employed consists of three men as factory maintenance staff.
And yet this is the plant which is equipped to manufacture the Bren machine gun. A question has been asked: What firms in Canada could make this gun? It is brought out in the report of the commission that a number of firms which are set out, such as the Dominion Bridge Company, Bertram Company, The Steel Company of Canada, Canadian Car and Foundry Company, Limited, the National Steel Company, and

Bren Gun- Mr. Marsh
others, are skilled in the manufacture of precision articles of steel of one kind or another, and that with very little additional tooling equipment could be harnessed to fulfil the contract.
It has been stated in the press that the Prime Minister and the cabinet were prepared to whitewash the department and had done so. I did not believe that when it came out in the press; I wanted to be fair and to see how the matter would be treated in this house. But since hearing the arguments yesterday and the day before, and again to-day, I am convinced that undoubtedly there has been an effort to whitewash the department. If that is so I would suggest that they bring in a brand-new barrel of whitewash if they have any hopes of restoring that pristine purity and whiteness from the present shade of tattle-tale gray. If this government has whitewashed the department and the minister, why has a purchasing board been advocated? Why another commission to be added to the multitudinous number of other commissions that have brought forth so much criticism from the taxpayers on former occasions?
I am not opposed to the appointment of a purchasing board, although I would much rather see a munitions board entirely devoid of political patronage. But in the establishment of a purchasing board or of a munitions board the government has found it necessary to take away from the department the power to purchase, which is a long piece removed from whitewashing. The point is that someone in the Department of National Defence, I know not who, authoritative enough, powerful enough to negotiate a contract, has made a sorry mess of things in this Bren gun contract. It is bad enough for the taxpayers of Canada to be dipping into their pockets and pulling out a million dollars a week for a publicly owned railroad; but it is doubly bad for money to be improvidently spent in a contract such as this, and I will tell you why. Underneath, overhead and all around every dollar spent in national defence may be the blood of Canadian young manhood. Mr. Speaker, I hesitated to rise in my place and condemn this contract. I believe throughout Canada to-day we must do everything possible to build up the faith of our people in such a department as the Department of National Defence. Had there been a time of crisis I should not have spoken, but perhaps it is best that this thing has come to light, so that other similar contracts may not be let. There are plenty of departments I would rather have attacked than the Department of National
Defence, for the reason that the people of Canada must be taught to have confidence in men in public places, and especially in this minister and this department.
While I am on my feet-and this does not particularly relate to the amendment-may I suggest that the government cannot economically and intelligently compete with private industry in the making of munitions. Our factories have lathes, milling machines, drills, shapers, punch presses, and so on. They have the necessary foundation work for precision machinery, and they have the necessary automatic machinery. So, with the possible exception of small arms, I think the government should not go into the munitions business. But may we make sure of this, that such business be let by contract, after tenders have been called, so that private industry may be allowed to compete. That is the only way we can buy munitions intelligently; and, contracts having been let, may every last piece, every last shell, every last machine and every last gun come up to specifications. This government and the Department of National Defence can see to it that there is no profiteering in connection with war materials.

After the discussion we have had here during the last two days, based on this blue book, during which the members on this side of the house have dealt essentially with the facts, while the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) dealt with a smoke screen and the hon, member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) entertained us in pantomime fashion, I suggest that there has been nothing wrong with the arguments presented from this side. If I understand the English language at all, as I read this report it is a condemnation of the government from cover to cover.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is the common thought of all that there should be no profiteering in Canada in connection with war supplies. What man can be called a Canadian who will make or take blood money? But here is a million dollars of profit on a stock transaction pertaining to a $5,000,000 contract. Is that economy? Is that a proper stewardship of money? Is that Canadian? I suggest that it is not, and I urge that this thing that has happened must not happen again.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with no previous knowledge of shell manufacture, using the broken down boiler factory that has been mentioned so often, using a cement factory and under similar conditions, Canadian manufacturers during

the last war produced munitions to the value of over a billion dollars. I joined the imperial munitions board shortly after the war started. I was superintendent of production; I think I know whereof I speak, and I may say that I have heard a good deal from the other side which to me is utter nonsense. Shell shipments from Canada increased from $5,377,000 in 1915 to $19,942,000 in 1916 and $23,782,000 in 1917. In 1917 we received orders to slow down in Canada, because we were shipping more munitions than they required. It was easier for me to speed up production than to slow it down, with my temperament, so I put in my resignation to the chairman, who paid me a tribute on the back of a cigarette case which I still carry occasionally, and which is inscribed with these words:
In grateful memory of unfailing support in a difficult task.
I left the munitions board, Mr. Speaker, thinking that the United States would want our production; and certainly our people who had been set going wanted to keep going. This was arranged. The Canadian government sent a trade board to Washington; I worked on my own, and I received the first order from the United States ordnance department for munitions to be made in Canada. The total of United States munitions contracts with Canada amounted to $232,168,000. Many of those contracts were cancelled because of the armistice, but shipments, to the United States, which commenced early in 1918, reached a total of seven million shells, in addition to two million shell forgings and other material. The total orders shipped from Canada by the imperial munitions board amounted to $1,200,672,412.78. In 1916 the total exports to the United Kingdom were $451,852,399.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Much has been said about the suitability of the John Inglis plant for the manufacture of Bren machine guns. I knew William Inglis in 1905, and for many years I did business with him. He was one of the first manufacturers to take an order from Sir Alexander Bertram to manufacture shells. What did he have then? He had the same boiler factory we have been talking about. I will pay this tribute to him, that he was a first class manufacturer, and did splendid work. When Mr. Inglis and other

Bren Gun-Mr. McAvity
gentlemen who undertook to manufacture shells, but who had never seen a shell before in their lives, took their first order, what did they do? They were practical men. They wanted to see a shell to see what it looked like. They wanted to visit factories to find out how shells were made. There was no difficulty about that, because it was very easy for Sir Sam Hughes and Sir Alexander Bertram to arrange for these gentlemen to go to the Quebec arsenal, where Colonel Lafferty showed them how shells were being made. They were shown only a few shells.
What happened in this case? Major Hahn wanted to manufacture Bren guns. What was the natural thing for him to ask? He wanted to see the gun made. First of all, he wanted to take it apart. He did that. He examined it, and then he went to England to see it made. I am asking if that is not what a practical man would have done. Is that not what a man who wishes to make an article he does not know much about would have done? Before he had gone very far he said, "I want to see the gun made." He went to England but could not gain admittance to the arsenal. Hon. members know what arsenals in the old country are like; it is difficult to get in. Nothing daunted, however, he went to the high commissioner's office and asked for a pass to gain admittance to the arsenal. That is all this amounts to, if one takes the trouble to read it through. The high commissioner cabled back, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) very properly replied. Surely no person can take exception to the cable, if he reads it in that light. It was a pass to the works at Enfield. That is the way I read it, and I believe that is exactly what was meant.
This whole matter has become befogged with a great mass of detail which confuses the ordinary man. I am not a lawyer, but it seems to me that was a perfectly reasonable and practical procedure, and the man did the right thing when he went to see the gun made. The manufacturer now in question is the type of man I would have selected to make shells in 1914, because it was just that type of man who produced results.
Frank P. Jones, president of the Canada Cement Company, operating a cement factory in Montreal, asked to be allowed to make shells. We gave him an order, and he was one of the best manufacturers we had. He did not have a factory at all; but he produced one, and in that factory he manufactured shells. He made special machinery, and was the first man to use female labour in
operating shell lathes on the heavy calibre 9-2 shells. I could mention a number of others who did the same thing, manufacturers who had had no experience but who, with no difficulty, became excellent production men.
To-day there is no factory in Canada equipped to manufacture the Bren gun. All the equipment must be created. So far as I have described the proceedings, surely this man has gone about the matter in the right way. Apparently Major Hahn went to England with a tentative order to make shells for the Canadian government. Although the order had not been signed at that time, at least he was expecting to get it. When he saw the gun being manufactured in the Enfield plant he was quite convinced he could make it and, what is more, convinced the British authorities as to his ability to do so. He developed a tentative order from them to make an additional 5,000 guns. In doing that be pointed out that by making 12.000 guns the price could be reduced to both Canadian and British governments. Surely there is nothing wrong with that.
Then Major Hahn returned to Canada- and what was he faced with? He was faced with an interdepartmental committee asking that tenders be called. At that stage of the game, I ask the house, how could tenders be called? It was an impossible proposition.

speechtext: Why, not?

speechtext: I will show why not: This man had won the confidence of the British war office, and had a tentative order from them for the manufacture of 5,000 guns. He also had a tentative order from the Canadian government for the manufacture of 7,000 guns. How could you put any other manufacturer in the same position, in the event of inviting competitive tenders?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Why, then, did the government appoint the interdepartmental committee?

I wish to return to the argument about the plant. There has been a great deal of talk about a broken down boiler factory. Let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite that it was not from the lists of old-time manufacturers, who had been in business for a hundred years or more, that the best manufacturers of shells were obtained. Those manufacturers were too conservative in their methods. I remember distinctly two firms in Brantford, namely, Gould, Shapely and Muir, and the Waterous engine works.
Bren Gun-Mr. McAvity

both with high standing, each of which received a comparatively large order from General Bertram for 50,000 of the 4-5 shells. In the same city of Brantford was the small firm of Kerr and Godwin, a firm which was almost unknown and one with less than a dozen employees on its payroll. Subsequently they secured an order from the shell committee for the manufacture of 10,000 shells. My memory as to the figures may not be exactly right, but I believe I am not far out. Kerr and Godwin had the right driving force. They got mechanics and machinery, and before the two well known firms had shipped 100,000 shells Kerr and Godwin had shipped 150,000. That is the type of firm we need to produce shells.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: What has that to do with this contract?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

You would not know,
anyway.

speechtext:
I did not hear the hon. member. The suggestion has been made that we should have a government arsenal. I believe the chief of staff suggested that an expenditure of between $30,000,000 and $35,000,000 should be made. Might I point out that an arsenal capable of producing a billion dollars worth of shells would cost a great deal more than $35,000,000. I would think it would cost something nearer $350,000,000-and wp certainly do not want to create any more white elephants of that kind to feed. It would be a white elephant in peace times.
I say we do not need an arsenal, and I believe that in continuing the practice we have followed we are following the practice of the rest of the world. Germany is mobilizing industry; France is mobilizing industry; the United States is mobilizing industry, and Canada must do the same.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Just one.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I pay tribute to the Department of National Defence for the work they have done. They have prepared a careful survey of all the manufacturing plants available in Canada. If a condition of war should arise again they will not be in such a muddle as that in which our Tory friends found themselves in 1915, when they were faced with the shell inquiry, the discarding of Oliver equipment, and other troubles. The Department of National Defence will have an organized plan through which it will be able to make use of industry, right from the start, and without any of the difficulties 
formerly experienced. In that connection I quote the words of Mr. David Lloyd George. He said:
Our eyes were at first shut to the vital importance of war material and the difficulty of improvising its production. The realization of what the enemy had done in this direction during years of stealthy preparation for the "day" came as a shock perhaps even greater than that caused by the discovery of his numerical strength, and was followed by the painful awakening as to what we had to undertake in order to catch up.
Certainly we are in a much better position 'to-day than we were in the fall of 1915 when our Tory friends were completely bewildered and confused by that rugged individualist Sir Sam Hughes who then had charge of affairs.
Much has been said of the cablegram which was sent, but as I have already said, it was nothing more or less than an application for a pass to permit Major Hahn to visit the Enfield works to inspect the manufacture of the gun. That is the way I read it. If my hon. friends opposite want an explanation of what happened in the last war, I would point out to them that the imperial munitions board was a branch of the imperial government headed by the Right Hon. David Lloyd George. Let me say to them that the then Prime Minister, Sir Robert L. Borden, came to our office to see our chairman with contractors and urging shell contracts for them. I think the same applied to every member of his government and almost every member of the house at that time. They were trying to get contracts from the imperial government. There is a precedent for you.
I have seen the contract which has been criticized by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens). I had a hand in making a thousand of contracts for munitions. I sat in and helped to make contracts with the imperial munitions board and the United States department of ordnance, and I never saw any contract which so rigidly ties down the manufacturer as does this Bren gun contract. Mr. Justice Davis rightly says:
No substantial objection can be taken in my view to the provisions of the Canadian contract.
I assume that no exception was taken to the provisions of the British contract. The commissioner says further:
There are adequate powers of inspection, supervision and control vested in the department.
In my opinion if the contract is rigidly enforced there will be little, if any, profit for Major Hahn and his associates. In connection with profits, and following my argument as to how a manufacturer with plenty

Bren Gun-Mr. McAvity
of force and vim who controls a large organization can carry out this work, let me refer to the late Sir Frank Baillie. What did he know about manufacturing munitions? What did he know about manufacturing anything before he was given an order for cartridge cases for the imperial munitions board? Yet he was one of the most successful and. most conscientious contractors that we had. When Lord Rhondda came to this country Sir Frank Baillie said to him that they were paying too much for these cartridge cases. He told him that if he was given an order for a million cases at the set price, he would turn back whatever profit he made after keeping accurate costs. These cases were costing $1.75 each; the order totalled $1,750,000, and he handed back $758,000.
A suggestion was made by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) that the railway shops should be turned into arsenals. I would point out to him that the railway shops were not used during the last war to any great extent for the simple reason that they were required in order to keep the locomotives and cars in running order. Transport is just as important as anything else.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: There is no war on just now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
But you do not want to have them manufacturing war materials and not be available if we do have a war. Since hon. gentlemen opposite have not made any constructive suggestions I should like to put on record one or two things which I believe could be profitably taken from our last experience in mobilizing industry.
I would urge upon the government the importance of not letting mechanics leave the country in the event of a crisis. We need all our mechanics for our mobilization scheme. Anyone can run a motor car, but how many can repair one? Similarly, anyone can run a shell machine, but how many can set one up? The hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding) knows all about that, because he was in the shell manufacturing business. If you have mechanics to set up these machines, if you have them tooled properly, a woman or a one-armed or one-legged man can run them. Then you would not need to hold back any volunteers or conscripts. But you must have mechanics and you must have foremen, because, like the sergeant in the army, the foreman is the backbone of any mobilization scheme.
Some valuable suggestions were made by the Hon. R. H. Brand, a member of the imperial munitions board. He resided in
England and maintained contact with the minister of munitions. In his report made after the war he had this to say:
In the first year or so of the war the possibilities of munitions making in Canada were not by any means fully recognized in England, and very large orders were placed in the United States which it would have been to everyone's interest to place in Canada. When once a huge program had been started in the United States it was a matter of some difficulty and many months to get it transferred to Canada. Other British departments similarly ignored the great assistance that Canada could be to them. For a good many months I urged unsuccessfully on the board of trade that Canada could build ships to assist in meeting the submarine crisis, and on the war office and the admiralty that Canada could provide not only aeroplanes but an air force. Even in December 1916 the board of trade informed me that they did not require any ships, and it was only after the ministry of shipping was formed that the board was authorized to begin a building program in Canada. Similarly it was only when the air board, the forerunner of the air ministry, was formed that serious attention was given to the possibilities of Canada in this direction. I was so convinced of the importance of this matter that I appeared before the air board to urge it at its first meeting. Shortly afterwards a program was agreed upon and the board was instructed to begin building aerodromes and aeroplanes.
If relations in future are to be close between the different governments of the empire-
That is why I am reading this because that is what we are interested in.
-and between different departments of those different governments, an effective liaison service will be absolutely necessary. The imagination and foresight of human beings are limited, and of civil servants as much as other classes of the community. If the imperial munitions board had had no representative of its own responsible to it, and there for the one purpose of interpreting its wishes and wants and difficulties to the ministry of munitions, friction would have been constant and inevitable. The officers of the ministry were overwhelmed with their own duties; they did not know Canada; they did not understand their problem, or their way of looking at matters; they did not realize that cable correspondence between men 3,000 miles apart is the most fruitful mother of misunderstanding. This is not said in any way to magnify the importance of my office. It is a fact. The trouble can easily be overcome by each department of each government having its own representative in close touch with it, and responsible to it to interpret its wishes in the other country.
I sincerely hope that the government will try to keep the authorities in England fully informed, either through the high commissioner's office or by some other means, as to our ability to produce shells. I hope that by some means or other this discussion on the Bren gun can be kept from their notice, because it certainly will not do us any good. We should point out to the British authorities that we are better prepared to-day
Bren Gun-Mr. McAvity

than ever before because we have made a complete survey of our industrial organization. We have more metals available to-day than ever before. The comparative figures in connection with zinc, nickel, lead and copper are quite surprising. I should like to give the figures for 1914, 1918 and 1937. I am giving the figures for 1918 to show that even under the pressure of war the supplies were comparatively low. The figures are:

I would just say in connection with this table that we have by long odds the largest nickel production in the w'orld. Lead, of course, is an important factor in the making of shrapnel, but most important of all the metals is copper, which is used for cartridge cases and fuses. In copper we were able to get up production only to 118,769,434 pounds in 1918, but the figure stands to-day at 531,041,878. So I say that we are in a much better position to-day than before, in that we have our own metals and our own mechanics, and our men will give a good account of ourselves.
There is one other item that I want to mention in connection with the whole problem of national defence, and it is a matter which I do not think has been seriously considered to date, I refer to the equipping of our more important ports so that in time of emergency certain specified terminals or areas can be completed on short notice for the use of the army, the navy and the air force without in any way disturbing the commercial activities of the port.
For many years the important United Kingdom and continental ports have always taken this problem into consideration in port development. In the United States, for the last thirty years or more, the United States army corps of engineers have had control of this problem. The policy developed by the United States government was to build army and navy base terminals at the more important ports. These terminals were leased to commercial enterprises during peace times, but could be taken over by the military authorities at once in the case of any crisis.
At practically all the terminals at the more important Canadian ports nothing has been done, and if it is found necessary to commandeer existing facilities for war purposes it will undoubtedly seriously disturb their commercial activities. Also these terminals
[Mr. McAvity. 1
are not equipped for operations under wartime conditions. The handling of high explosive munitions and supplies of one kind or another is a highly technical matter, and, particularly with respect to munitions, a dangerous operation. We certainly should not risk a repetition of the Halifax explosion.
It seems to me very important that in the scheme of national defence the situation with regard to port and terminal facilities at our national ports should be reviewed, and operating orders should be in the hands of a responsible person so that the various harbours involved would be able to change over from ordinary commercial harbours to a war-time basis without the inconvenience that was experienced during the last war.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to approach this delicate subject in as dispassionate a tone and tenor as possible. Like the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) it is not my intention to be personal, and I hope that no one in the house, neither the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) nor any other member, will construe the remarks I may have to make as in any way reflecting on their personal character or characteristics. I have a public duty to perform, and I shall endeavour to perform it to the best of my ability. If I err in my judgment I know that my constituency will hold me responsible. Human flesh is subject to the frailties of conditions and times, and in a moment of weakness we are all likely to make errors which later we attempt to retract.
I was hoping that as this debate progressed we might observe some symptoms from the government benches of light beginning to dawn, some indications that they realized that a serious mistake had been made and were prepared to remedy a condition that was not conducive to the good of Canada. It was my privilege, Mr. Speaker, to be in attendance for several sessions at the Bren gun inquiry, and I had the opportunity of observing the various witnesses and noting the remarks made by counsel and from the bench. In speaking on this subject I am therefore not totally unaware of the subject matter of the report; for I have had the privilege of reading it, and noting very carefully some particulars of it, and I also had the privilege of listening to the testimony that was given before the commissioner from time to time.
This is serious matter that we are discussing. I do not think anyone in the house will gainsay that statement. A condition has grown up which, unfortunately, must be rectified.

Bren Gun-Mr. Walsh
The Bren gun was first discussed. I understand, back in 1936. The defence department became interested in it, and later, in 1938, after a lapse of almost two years, a contract was entered into with a firm known as John Inglis Company Limited to manufacture Bren guns for the government of Canada and for the British war office. I should like for a moment or two to strip this whole undertaking of its frills, verbal and otherwise, and examine the bald facts in connection with the Bren gun transaction.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: You will have to answer all the speeches made on the other side, then.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am fortunate. Mr. Speaker, in that I have little to answer from the other side of the house. They have put up very little argument as yet, although most of the speakers on the other side, I notice, have been very astute lawyers, able to defend a type of case where the going is rather difficult. I commend the government for their ability to raise speakers of that type and press them into service. But what we should like to hear from the other side is a definite argument to offset those which have been advanced from this side. The facts and figures in connection with this contract have been very impressively placed on record, but they have not been dealt with by speakers on the other side of the house. Anyone who has been reading Hansard for the past two or three days, with any degree of non-bias, will readily agree that the speeches of hon. gentlemen on the other side have been made, not in defence of the contract entered into, not to combat the statements made from this side of the house, but merely to gloss over the conditions as they really exist. They have made a vain attempt to apply a coat of veneer to a rough and unfinished surface, and that coat is not sticking, as they will realize when they confront their public.
Let us now examine this Bren gun contract. The government decided that they would manufacture and use this Bren gun. A person was selected, Major Hahn. As any business corporation or organization would do in a delicate proposition of this kind, one involving the spending of millions of money, one would think the government would be very careful to select a person or organization equipped in every way to handle the contract they were seeking to place. But, instead of that careful investigation, instead of selecting an established firm or an individual who was qualified technically and otherwise to handle a matter of this kind, they selected Major Hahn.

He understands certain
features of the industry, but he does not understand the Bren gun or the Bren gun contract. That is what we are discussing. And we are discussing this contract in the light of to-day, not in the light of experience of twenty or twenty-five years ago. Major Hahn had a splendid war record; he had one experience in business, namely the manufacture of radios; that was his qualification to apply for the contract for the manufacture of Bren guns. He did not even have a plant; he had no equipment; he had nothing whatsoever to commend him to the Department of National Defence except a recommendation from the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton). With that recommendation he obtained the ear of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), of the deputy minister of national defence, and he obtained the entree into channels on the other side that finally led to his getting the contract.
Mention has been made in this debate of the attitude of the British war office. I leave it to hon. members on both sides of the house; here was a man who went to England with official introductions and who received through the high commissioner's office other letters of introduction. He was accompanied by a Liberal member of the Canadian parliament, accompanied also by the brother of that member, a lawyer. He was also blessed, as few other people are blessed, with official recognition by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), a recognition which very few people in this country could obtain. I wish to read again this cablegram from the Department of External Affairs, over which the Prime Minister presides, which gave Major Hahn his official introduction. Hon .members must bear in mind that Major Hahn was in London; the war office in London refused to interview him except in the presence of an official of this dominion, and in order to consolidate his position over there, in order

Bren Gun-Mr. Walsh
to facilitate his entree, this cablegram was dispatched. It may be found at page 24 of the royal commissioner's report:
Secret. Your cablegram 9th November 396. Have discussed matter with Minister of National Defence. You might request war office to give Major Hahn, as representing Canadian government-
Mark that.
-as representing Canadian government in this particular, any information which they consider desirable and necessary to enable National Defence to reach conclusion on possibility produce Bren gun in Canada. It is not desired to request furnishing of information on any article other than this gun.
There he was, officially recognized, a potential contractor, a man who was seeking to obtain a contract from our government. This cablegram was dispatched from the Department of External Affairs, no doubt at the instigation of the Prime Minister. Major Hahn was there under those circumstances. Can one imagine a business firm conducting an important piece of business in that way, to a potential contractor, one seeking favours, an official introduction and hence an entree into the very heart of the empire and to establish his standing? My hon. friends on the other side say, we could not do very much; he was the man selected by the British war office. The British war office would never have selected Major Hahn but for the recommendation of the Minister of National Defence and the Prime Minister of Canada. Major Hahn would never have obtained entree to the war office in Great Britain if he had not had this recommendation and had not been officially endorsed as a representative of this country by the Prime Minister, who did it after consulting with the Minister of National Defence.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

I may say, so far as I am concerned, I have the utmost trust and faith that this is a good contract for the people of Canada, because I am sure that the war office people and the British people, with their wonderful experience, knowledge and training would not enter into a contract which was not for the public good. If hon. members will look at the minutes of that committee they will see that there was a marked conflict of opinion as between the chairman and the other members of the committee.

speechtext:
As I always do, I accept
the word of the minister unreservedly. I do not desire to put on the record anything that cannot be regarded as a truthful statement.
I was very much surprised, and, indeed, hurt, when the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Bertrand) dragged into the debate the suggestion that it was being carried on with a view to casting a reflection on a French-Canadian. Surely the hon. gentleman did not intend to convey such an impression. I have known the hon. member for Laurier as crown prosecutor in Montreal for many years, and he has lived as a neighbour of mine for a considerable time. I am absolutely certain that he had no intention of deliberately raising the race cry in a matter of this kind. I hope he will take advantage of the first opportunity to retract a suggestion that can only lead to disunity in Canada. We all know that we need more unity and harmony than we have at the present time. I say,

Mr. Speaker, I have been keenly interested in the debate on the Bren machine gun in which hon. members from both sides of the house have taken part. May I in the first place congratulate the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. McAvity) upon the very excellent, clear and lucid statement of facts which set at naught in a businesslike way many of the attacks made by hon. members opposite. As he has dealt with arguments of hon. members opposite in a definite manner I shall deal with an aspect of the contract which so far as I know has not been mentioned in the house.
As yet no credit has been given to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) for using his judgment in picking the Bren machine gun. I find considerable criticism of the contract by hon. members opposite, and may I say in passing that I believe they would have been fairer if they had mentioned that the minister had picked probably the finest machine gun in the world, and one which has been adopted by the British army. We find this at page 4 of the report:
What is known as the Bren gun is a light machine gun, a weapon invented and patented in Czecho-SIovakia. The information given the commission was that the weapon which eventually became the Bren gun was demonstrated to the British government in 1930. It was then known as ZB 26. It was introduced by the Czecho-Slovakian firm and was brought to the attention of the British and was tried out in England. There were several details in the
fun which had to be modified to conform to tritish conditions. Between 1930 and 1935 the gun was modified and changed and eventually became the Bren gun in its present form, and during that period it was subjected to very severe tests in England the result of which was that it was considered satisfactory and suitable for the purposes of light automatics better than anything else available.
The suitability of the said machine gun and the urgency of its purchase or production for the use of the defence forces of Canada was common ground with all parties represented before the commission.
In view of that statement in the report it is hard to understand how hon. members
opposite could endorse the suggestion that the Inglis plant should be closed down for months, when they are engaged in the manufacture of machine guns for the British and Canadian governments.
After the contract was signed attacks were made through Maclean's magazine, and by Colonel George Drew, speaking throughout the country. As a result of those attacks a royal commission was finally asked for. The request for the commission was promptly acceded to by the Prime Minister-probably a lot more quickly than some of the critics had hoped. What do we find? The powers given to the commissioner were wide; there was no attempt by the Prime Minister or the government to restrict the course of the inquiry. On the contrary they welcomed a full investigation. One of the terms of reference stated the commissioner was to report as speedily as possible to the governor in council the result of his investigation, together with the evidence taken before him, and any opinion he might see fit to express thereon. I believe hon. members of the opposition must agree that the Prime Minister and the government took the right attitude in granting a commission, and gave ample powers to the commissioner appointed.
Was the commissioner satisfactory? One of our most respected judges, the Hon. Henry Hague Davis of the Supreme Court of Canada, was named commissioner. I do not believe hon. members opposite can find any fault with his appointment. He was called to the bench by a former administration, and I do not think hon. members can claim that during the hearing of the evidence there was any tendency towards protecting the Minister of National Defence. All members must be satisfied in that respect.
Let me say this to hon. members. When they criticize the Minister of National Defence they should take into account the conditions existing in the world at this time and the condition in which the minister found the department when this government assumed office in 1935. So that hon. members of this house and the people of this country may know of some of the troubles with which the minister had to contend in his efforts to protect this country from attack, I think there should be put on record the condition of the Department of National Defence when the previous government left office. The minister is in his seat and I ask him to correct me if I am inaccurate in any statement I make in regard to the efficiency or lack of efficiency of the defence services of this country.
I shall deal first with the naval service. Barracks, dock yards and shore equipment
Bren Gun-Mr. Mulock

were antiquated and inadequate. The naval magazine at Esquimalt had been condemned as far back as 1905.
In the militia service there was not a single anti-aircraft gun, although four had been ordered the year before by the previous government. In field gun ammunition the stock was less than ninety minutes' firing for guns inherited from 1918, less than half the "equipment ammunition" supposed to travel with the guns. There were no reserves. The field artillery was unsuited for mechanical traction and was outranged by from 3,000 to 6.000 yards. The coast defence armaments were obsolescent and defective. Firing practices had been curtailed, these instructions having been given in order to save the guns. The gunners were not receiving proper training. In the mechanical transport there were only a few tractors for permanent force batteries. There were no tanks or armoured cars, and no tractors for heavy guns or non-permanent field batteries. In connection with anti-gas defence there were not sufficient gas masks for the permanent force, and there were none for mobilization. No steps had been taken to provide other forms of anti-gas defence. There were no manufacturing facilities in Canada for the production of rifles, machine guns or artillery. The dominion arsenal was equipped only to manufacture rifle ammunition and a limited amount of field ammunition.
The reorganization of the militia had been recommended in 1932 and approved by the government, but no steps had been taken in the matter. Militia training had been so much restricted that many officers had had no experience in commanding troops on manoeuvres, nor had they had the opportunity to acquire the power of leadership by actual practice. The training of officers and non-commissioned officers in administrative duties had been neglected, and the majority of men in the ranks had had little or no experience in handling rifles. The training efficiency was approximately 17 per cent.
We come now to the air service. There were only twenty-three aircraft of service type, all obsolescent. None are suitable for active service to-day and are useful only for training. There were no air bombs available in Canada for immediate use. There were no aero engines, and the development of an industry would take two years. No steps had been taken in connection with industrial mobilization to survey the country's industrial resources for national defence.
During the Brandon by-election the government was charged with being a " do-nothing government." Now certain hon. members

are criticizing this government and the Minister of National Defence for doing something. May I point out that in 1930-31 the combined votes for the three defence services of this country amounted to $22,163,500, and in 1933-34 they had been reduced to $13,002,484. The vote for air services was reduced from $7,475,700 to $1,697,000 in the same period. These are some of the things with which the Minister of National Defence had to deal. I think everyone will agree that he had a lot of trouble on his hands when he took over the department, which to say the least was not in the best of condition.
In making this contract he had the advice of loyal and experienced men. I assume they were loyal and experienced as many of them had been appointed under former administrations. I think he had a right to rely on the advice of the interdepartmental committee. If you condemn the Minister of National Defence, at the same time you must condemn the interdepartmental committee.

Since this debate started there has been an attempt, not only in this house but outside, to create a more or less political villain. Unfortunately the person through whom the government was to be attacked is the Minister of National Defence. In times like these I think criticism might well be tempered with a realization of the conditions prevailing throughout the world and the fact that all democracies are now threatened with demands by totalitarian states. It seems to me to be a sad reflection on our democratic system to see dictatorships going ahead with their arming while we in this House of Commons are arguing over where we are going to get some guns. Surely there can be no doubt in the minds of the people of the danger that threatens this country, the British empire, and all the democracies. We all hope and pray that we shall never see again the condition that existed during the last war. We all hope and pray that this country will never be plunged into another war, but at the same time I do not think that the democratic peoples of the world are prepared to bow the knee to the dictatorships, whether they be nazi or communist.
We are hearing every day of the great preparations being made by the war machines of the world. May I say to hon. members that Germany can lose a war and recover, but

Bren Gun-Mr. Young
the British empire can lose only one war. Then the empire would be split up. I think we would be much better occupied in this House of Commons in trying to expedite the preparations to defend ourselves from attack than in stirring up these bickerings over what form of contract there should be for the supplying of machine guns.

YOUNG (Saskatoon): Mr. Speaker, as this is the first time that I have spoken in the house this year I should like to congratulate my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) upon being elected the leader of his party. I have been very much interested, as have all hon. members, in the discussion which has been taking place in the house during the last week. I was interested in the article appearing in Maclean's magazine, written by Colonel George Drew. An advance copy of the article had been sent to me, I assume because it was thought I did not read the magazine at all, and the first impression I gained was that apparently the magazine itself was anxious to have some such propaganda to increase its circulation. The second thing which struck me was that there must have been some necessity compelling Colonel Drew to write the article, and later on it developed that there was. There was an
island over there upon which stood the Conservative citadel. He wanted to get into that citadel, and his article was the approach, what might be called the Drew bridge, over which he hoped to reach the citadel. Later on he was elected leader of the Conservative patry in Ontario, and so far as I am concerned it will always be my belief that this article was written in order that he might get the publicity he required to place him in that position.
When I first read the article I was inclined to approach it, as I do a great many other matters, in a critical attitude. I never believe in accepting anything from any source without first investigating for myself whether or not the contract is a good one.
Perhaps I might explain to the house why I was more critical in this matter than usual. I remembered that we had a war before. I remember the contracts that were given in that last war. I remember the horse contracts; I remember the boot contracts; I remember the shovel contracts; I remember the bacon contracts; I remember the potato contracts; I remember the munitions contracts; I remember that all these contracts were given to people in Canada without any proper supervision, and that enormous profits were made out of these contracts, and I declared then, and I have declared ever since, that it should be absolutely understood in connection with any more war or munitions contracts to be placed by this country every possible safeguard against undue profits must be taken.
What happened later, after those contracts had been given?-and I would like to remind my hon. friends opposite of this. After all those vultures had gathered together their profits from those contracts the government of that day, not content with that, and when everybody else in the dominion was getting poorer and poorer every day, gave to these people wrho had made such tremendous profits out of munitions contracts of one kind or another, the opportunity to buy tax-free bonds, so that the country was not able to get back any of the money which these people had taken. It is little wonder therefore, Mr. Speaker, after the experience we have already had with war contracts, that we should be critical of any contract for munitions or war supplies given by any government at this particular time.
There has been some criticism made of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for his appointment of the judge as commissioner, and who that judge was. Let me say this, that the Prime Minister was not fearful of
Bren Gun-Mr. Young

appointing a judge whom he himself and his government had previously appointed. Not that at all, but I say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to every hon. member, that had a judge who had been appointed by the Prime Minister been chosen to head the commission investigating the Bren gun contract, the very first thing we should have heard from this country would have been that a commissioner had been appointed who had previously been appointed by the Prime Minister himself. Is there any hon. member who doubts that?
Let me give the house my experience before even the judge was flamed. I heard in the constituency in which I live, and I heard of it in other constituencies, that in all probability a judge of that kind would be appointed who would do the bidding of the Prime Minister and of the government. Let me go further and say that after the present judge was appointed the commissioner-and he is a judge with as fine a record and character as can be found in this country-before they knew his political persuasion, some people were saying: Well, this man having been appointed by the present Prime Minister you can be prepared for a report of the kind that the present government would like. When I pointed out to them that the circumstances did not happen to be as they thought, that the commissioner had not been appointed a judge by the present government, they were confounded. But if someone else had been appointed you would" have heard the same kind of talk from coast to coast, just as surely as we are sitting here debating this matter to-day.
To touch on one or two points that have come up in this debate, criticism has been made of the reply that was given by the minister to a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). The question asked at that time was answered correctly. It was answered, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) said, "poisonously accurately." I wonder what kind of answer hon. members expect. Do they expect correct answers to questions asked? I would say this to any hon. member who criticizes that answer, that perhaps they are suggesting that the government should anticipate that hon. gentlemen do not ask the questions which they really desire to ask and that they should be given answers sought in spite of their own stupidity; in other words, that they were not sufficiently capable of putting the questions which they wished to ask. Surely no hon. member would criticize the minister or anyone else for giving a correct answer to the question which was asked.

There has also been criticism of the letter which the minister gave' to Major Hahn, and which is referred to on page 17 of the commissioner's report. It is dated October 19, 1936, and reads:
Dear Mr. Massey:
The bearer of this letter, Major J. E. Hahn, D.S.O., M.C., is in England to investigate the manufacture of all classes of munitions and armaments.
Again I ask, is there any hon. member in this chamber; is there any person in this country who would take even the slightest exception to a letter of that kind? I am informed that many others have had similar letters on many occasions. If any hon. member takes exception to that, let him now rise in his place or for ever after hold his peace. Yet the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) is criticized for giving that letter. Mr. Speaker, there is no answer.

My hon. friend who just interrupted me pointed out where he thought there was some stock manipulation.

Whether the plant cost 81,000,000 or 8100,000,000 cannot add one cent to the cost of the guns, because there is a stated specific cost per foot for the factory space used in the production of the Bren machine gun, and that amount of space occupied will be under the control of the Department of National Defence. It cannot possibly add one dollar to the cost, no matter what suggestions my hon. friends may try to put forth lor the people of this country. If there was any stock manipulation

of which I know nothing-that is not going to cost the people of this country anything.

Well, I do, Mr. Speaker.
I am sorry if there are so many hon. gentlemen who do not seem to understand anything.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I have seen in this house in the last few days a most astounding spectacle. I have been here for a number of years, and there are certain principles and practices and rules of procedure that are observed. Whenever anything comes up that hon. members want fully investigated and all facts brought out, what do we do? We appoint a committee and refer the matter to it in order that all the facts and relevant information may be disclosed. My hon. friends
try to suggest tha/t the evidence is in the report of the commission. Certainly there is some evidence there, but there are so many things not before the commission, as exemplified in this debate, that the only way to get them is to send this report to the committee. But what have my hon. friends done? They have done everything they possibly can, within and without the rules, to prevent this from going to the committee. Why? Because they know that at this time the Bren gim is being made, in spite of what they are saying, and the last thing in the world hon. members want to know is the whole of the facts in regard to this contract. Why? The other day the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) made a motion, which the government accepted, and what was the result? Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friends voted against your ruling that their amendment was out of order. If the challenge to your ruling had been successful, what would have happened? The logical conclusion is that if the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) had carried they would have destroyed the very motion that they themselves wanted passed. [DOT]
Let us be honest; let us be sincere; let us face facts as we should face them. If hon. members really believe that this is a bad contract, let it go to the committee where all the facts can be brought out and later brought before the house and before all the people of this country, and let the contract be judged on its merits. But apparently that is not what hon. members opposite want. They want to make it appear that this commission arrived at no full and final conclusion with regard to the contract. Did the commissioner say that there was anything wrong with the contract? Nothing wrong whatever. Have any hon. members opposite who have spoken found anything wrong with the contract? Nothing whatever. Did the commissioner find any evidence of graft or corruption anywhere?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: There was no charge of graft or corruption.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
That is the trouble, there is no charge about anything, nothing but accusations and insinuations. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Marsh) said that we had to whitewash the government. What did he mean? Did he mean that there has been so much mud-slinging in the last few days that a little whitewash was needed? There has been nothing but accusations and insinuations; no evidence of any kind at any time that hon. members were trying to analyze the contract and find out whether it
70S
Bren Gun-Mr. Young

is bad or good, or whether any hon. member in connection with the contract had not done his full duty. The people of this country will judge what the intent of the opposition really is. If the intent were to find out whether or not this was a good contract, what was the obvious thing to do? Every hon. member would be voting to send it to the committee in order that all the facts could be brought out and everyone would know them. But of course they do not want that. One or two hon. members went back to Toronto and then came here and said that others would have taken this contract. I think that is true. But how was the contract given to Major Hahn? As the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) said last night, Major Hahn has a fine war record, a fine character, is an able executive. He went to the Department of National Defence and saw a gun standing there, mounted. He said, what is this? He looked at it and right there his genius was displayed, because he believed he could make that gun. So he asked the department to have it sent to Toronto where he might investigate it further.
Then he went to the old country; he wanted to have access there to see how the gun was made, and after having seen the gun made he concluded that he could make it in Canada. Then what did he do? He impressed the British government with his ability, a government that has been entering into contracts of this type for years and years, hundreds of years; he "sold himself" to the British government, and succeeded in getting a contract for 5,000 guns from them. Then what? Supposing there were some bad faith about it, would he then have asked for the loan of a man who had been doing this work in a British factory for the last thirty-eight years to take charge of a plant here and have first-hand supervision of the whole operation? That is not the action of a man who was trying to do a wrong thing by this country. There is every evidence that he went about the matter in the most businesslike way in order that he might do, not only for this dominion, but for the British government, the finest piece of work a man could perform.
One serious thing about this discussion is this. In Canada, where there is a great deal of unemployment, we have under this contract the first opportunity of making some munitions for the British government, and the discussion that has taken place in this house will tend to discourage more of the same thing. This discussion will have a greater influence in that direction than anything

else, and the Conservative party will be responsible. They have taken upon their own shoulders a load of responsibility which they will not be able to shake off.
I believe that we have here in Canada tne brains, ability, material and machinery, to do a great deal of this manufacturing, and if the once great Conservative party, the present party being a mere remnant of its former self, had been assisting in the good work rather than trying to hinder it they would have shown themselves much better citizens than they have been demonstrated to be.
This is a serious time. A few years ago I would not have been found declaring in this house that we ought to be making munitions, because I thought then that the possiblity of war was entirely removed from the nations of the earth. But with thousands of others who think as I do I say that it is incumbent upon us to build up our national defences. Therefore, it is a sorry sight to see the great National Conservative party spoiling every chance we have in this country of improving our own condition. While I hope that there will never be any use for these implements of war, at the same time I sincerely hope that if war comes we shall not be found wanting as we were many years ago.
I should very much like to feel that in a matter of great importance to the country, such as this, we could have had. the Liberal government could have had, the full cooperation of all hon. members. It is most unfortunate, however, that we find hon. members opposite doing everything they can to frustrate any effort that is made. When this question went before the royal commission an exhaustive investigation was held. The commission sat for many weeks, and what was the verdict? It can be summed up in the last sentence or two of the report in which the commissioner says:
I think it right to say that there is no evidence (nor is there in the evidence any ground for suspicion) that the minister or the deputy minister or any officer or official of the Department of National Defence was guilty of any act of corruption or anything in the nature of corruption.
In other words, the commissioner said, "I find no fault with this man," echoing the greatest words ever pronounced in the most solemn tribunal that ever sat in this world. And what do we find immediately afterwards? We find that the Tory rabble from coast to coast cries, "Crucify this man!" The leader of the opposition introduces a motion asking that we crucify the contract, and the second stage would be to "crucify the minister," notwithstanding that the commissioner has de-

Broadcasting Privilege
dared that he finds no fault with him. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) would have the minister crucified right now. I say, Mr. Speaker, that we are fortunate in having as Minister of National Defence the type of man who is at present the head of that department. I am in a position to say that last September, after getting out of a sick bed, I journeyed to Ottawa and called on my good friend the minister in his room at the hotel. My wife was with me. In the report the commissioner recommends a board, and hon. gentlemen opposite have tried to suggest that this reference is unfortunate so far as the Minister of National Defence is concerned. What did the Minister of National Defence say to me in his room in September? He said, "Doctor Young, if there is one thing I would detest more than anything else it is that in any contract with which I have anything to do there should be any undue profit from any source, and I think it would be a fine thing to have some board established to which all these contracts could be sent instead of having them dealt with by the minister." That was his suggestion last September, and there is nothing in the report that was not already suggested to me by the minister himself. Does that suggest that he himself wishes to control any part of munitions contracts in order that he might do something which might not be recognized as proper? I submit the evidence is that he absolutely desired the very thing which the commissioner reported and the government accepted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me a fair question? Will he give any reason why the minister did not make that suggestion to the commissioner?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend the reason. My colleagues will bear me out that I placed the suggestion before them at the time, and discussed with the Prime Minister the possibility of making the suggestion to the commissioner, but I thought as a responsible minister of the crown it was not my place to make such a recommendation to a responsible commissioner.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: My hon. friend opposite is paying me a compliment when he suggests that I could read what was in the minister's mind.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext: You read ours. I do not know why you could not read the minister's.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION FOR REFERENCE TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If there was any time in the history of our country when we should not 71492-49
have such a frivolous discussion as this, that time is now; and if hon. gentlemen are sincere in saying that they wish to know all about this contract, the proper thing for them to have done was to support the motion to have the matter go to the committee so that we would have known exactly what the situation was.
It is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
